name: Release v0.10.1
body:
A patch release. It fixes the disk encryption type on default Fedora
Workstation installs, keeps the policy stream alive across a suspend,
unblocks SELinux constraints in custom modules, and publishes signed
checksums with every release. No database migrations, no configuration
changes.

## Bug Fixes

### Disk Encryption

- **LUKS volumes behind a btrfs root are discovered again.** btrfs (and
  bcachefs) mounts carry an anonymous device number in `mountinfo`, so
  `/sys/dev/block` has no node for them and the walk to the dm-crypt
  container never started. On a default Fedora Workstation install the root
  volume was invisible: `bor-agent luks status` printed no volumes,
  `bor-agent luks adopt` found nothing, and the encryption check reported
  the root as unencrypted. The agent now resolves the mount source to its
  block node when the device number is anonymous.
- **zram swap is compliant.** RAM-backed swap never reaches a disk, yet the
  system-scope encryption check reported it as an unencrypted swap device,
  which made every default Fedora Workstation install non-compliant. Such
  devices are flagged during discovery and reported as compliant with the
  reason.
- **The LUKS inventory flag reaches agents.** `AgentConfig.disk_encryption_inventory`
  is documented as on by default, but the server never set it, so a node
  without a bound `DiskEncryption` policy reported no volumes and the Disk
  Encryption page stayed empty until a policy bound. The server now sends it
  as true.
- **`bor-agent luks adopt` prompts on the terminal.** `systemd-ask-password`
  only uses the TTY when stdin is one, and the generic command runner
  detaches the child, so adoption fell back to the password-agent protocol:
  a wall broadcast, with the typed passphrase echoed by the terminal. The
  tool now runs with the caller's stdin and stderr, and prints a hint when
  stdin is not a terminal. Adoption also reports the inventory before asking
  for the passphrase, so adopting a fresh node no longer fails with "LUKS
  volume not found" because the server had not yet learned the volume.
- **A recovery-key rotation no longer breaks the protector binds that follow
  it.** Rotation wipes the old Bor recovery slots once the new key is
  confirmed. Where the credential for the sync came from a server release
  (the active recovery key, handed out for a pending rotation), it stopped
  opening the volume the moment the rotation finished and the Tang bind right
  after it failed with "Error adding new binding". A reveal with
  rotate-after-reveal on a Tang-bound node hit this on every sync. Rotation
  now returns the key it enrolled and the sync continues with that credential
  for TPM 2.0, Tang and bootstrap retirement.
- **Adding a Tang server works.** `Settings -> Tang Servers -> Add` failed
  with an internal error because a new record was inserted with a nil
  `advertised_thumbprints` array, which PostgreSQL rejects for the NOT NULL
  column. A nil list is stored as an empty one.

### Policy Streaming

- **The agent notices a dead policy connection.** After a suspend and resume,
  a NAT reset or a server restart, the node's TCP socket to the policy port
  can stay established while the server has already dropped the connection
  (its TCP user timeout fires as soon as a push goes unacknowledged for 20
  seconds). The agent then waited in `Recv` on a stream that no longer existed
  and saw no new bindings until it was restarted. The client now sends HTTP/2
  keepalive pings every 60 seconds with a 20 second timeout, which closes such
  a connection and lets the existing reconnect loop take over. The server's
  enforcement policy permits pings every 10 seconds.

### SELinux

- **Custom modules may use `constrain`.** The CIL statement allowlist rejected
  it, which ruled out the one statement that can take a permission away from
  the unconfined domains (they hold allow rules for everything), so a module
  that keeps a service from being killed from a shell could not be authored.
  Constraints restructure nothing in the base policy, and a bad one is undone
  by removing the module. Statements that do restructure the base policy
  (classes, sids, users and roles, MLS, policy capabilities, kernel object
  contexts) are still refused.

## Security

- **The agent runs with an MCS category of its own on SELinux systems.** The
  packaged unit sets `SELinuxContext=-system_u:system_r:unconfined_service_t:s0:c1023`,
  so the agent keeps its unconfined service domain but gets the level
  `s0:c1023`. The category confines nothing by itself: on the targeted policy
  MCS binds only container domains for file access. It lets an SELinux policy
  single the agent process out without a module per node, for example with a
  `constrain` statement that refuses signals from senders at a lower level, so
  that `kill -9` from a root shell is denied while
  `systemctl restart bor-agent` keeps working. The leading `-` makes systemd
  ignore a policy that lacks the type, and the directive is skipped where
  SELinux is disabled. Documented in the hardening guide and on the SELinux
  policy type page.

## Packaging & CI

- **Signed `SHA256SUMS` with every release.** A publish-checksums job runs
  once the agent and server packages of a GitHub release are uploaded. It
  assembles `SHA256SUMS` from the digests GitHub records for the assets
  (downloading and hashing only where a digest is missing), signs it with the
  release key that also signs the package repositories, verifies the signature
  and uploads `SHA256SUMS` and `SHA256SUMS.asc` to the release.

## Upgrade Notes

- **No database migrations and no new settings.** Server and agent
  configuration from v0.10.0 is unchanged.
- **Server and agent can be upgraded independently.** The Tang server,
  SELinux `constrain` and LUKS inventory fixes are server-side; the volume
  discovery, zram, `luks adopt`, rotation-credential and keepalive fixes are
  agent-side. Upgrade both to get all of them.
- **The agent package replaces `bor-agent.service`** to add the
  `SELinuxContext=` directive. Local changes belong in a drop-in under
  `/etc/systemd/system/bor-agent.service.d/`; a modified unit file in
  `/usr/lib/systemd/system/` is overwritten by the package.
- **Nodes whose LUKS volumes were invisible report them after the agent
  upgrade.** Once discovery works, the inventory arrives within 15 minutes and
  previously missing volumes appear on the Disk Encryption page, where they can
  be adopted.

name: Release v0.10.0
body:
# Release v0.10.0

## Licensing

- **Bor is now licensed under the AGPL-3.0-only** (it was LGPL-3.0-or-later).
  Contributions require a signed Contributor License Agreement, handled on
  the pull request. Vute Tech LTD also distributes Bor Enterprise under a
  commercial license.

## New Features

### Disk Encryption Policy Type

- **Disk encryption (`DiskEncryption`, shown as LUKS)** is a new policy type
  that manages LUKS2 full-disk encryption across the fleet. A policy names
  the volumes in scope, requires them to be encrypted, enrolls unattended
  unlocking through the **TPM 2.0** chip (`systemd-cryptenroll`, explicit
  PCR profiles) and/or **Tang** network servers (`clevis`, pinned signing
  keys the administrator confirmed), and escrows a per-volume **recovery
  key** on the Bor server. Bor never converts a disk: an unencrypted volume
  is reported as non-compliant.
- **The server is never in the boot path.** Unlocking is done by the
  initramfs (TPM, Tang or a typed recovery key); a server outage never stops
  a machine from booting. The agent runs `cryptsetup`, `systemd-cryptenroll`
  and `clevis` with fixed arguments and passes key material on stdin or a
  dedicated pipe, never on a command line or in a file, and zeroes it after
  use.
- **Escrow you can trust.** Recovery keys are sealed per record with
  AES-256-GCM under a key-encryption key (KEK) read from a file outside the
  database (`BOR_ESCROW_KEK_FILE`), with the volume, LUKS UUID, record and
  KEK id bound as additional data. Escrow is a two-phase commit (escrow
  first, confirm after the keyslot exists), rotation is crash-resumable, and
  the KEK rotates through `BOR_ESCROW_KEK_PREVIOUS_FILES` with a background
  rewrap. Without a KEK the feature stays off (fail closed).
- **Help-desk recovery.** The new **Disk Encryption** page shows the fleet
  summary, a volume search and the per-node detail. Revealing a recovery key
  needs the `disk_encryption:reveal` permission (Super Admin only by
  default), a reason or ticket number, and a fresh re-authentication with
  the password and an authenticator code (step-up; the code is mandatory
  while `BOR_ESCROW_REQUIRE_MFA` is on, the default). Every reveal and every
  refusal is audited (`recoverykey.reveal`, `recoverykey.reveal_denied`). Retired keys stay
  revealable for `BOR_ESCROW_RETIRED_RETENTION_DAYS` (30) and the keys of
  deleted nodes for `BOR_ESCROW_ORPHAN_RETENTION_DAYS` (90), then they are
  crypto-shredded.
- **Tang servers** are registered under **Settings -> Tang Servers**: the
  server fetches and verifies the advertisement (JWS over ES512), pins the
  RFC 7638 SHA-256 thumbprints, probes the servers periodically and reports a
  key change (`tangserver.check`).
- **Inventory and drift.** Agents report every LUKS2 volume with its keyslots
  and tokens every 15 minutes; keyslot fingerprints detect drift and cloned
  disks (`luks.drift`, `luks.clone_suspected`, `luks.tpm_reseal`). The node
  drawer gains a disk encryption section and the Compliance page labels the
  LUKS items.
- **Adopt existing machines** with `bor-agent luks status` and `bor-agent
  luks adopt`, which inspect the volumes and enroll the Bor protectors with
  an existing passphrase, interactively and under a lock file. New machines
  are provisioned through a one-time bootstrap credential directory.
- **Permissions** `disk_encryption:view` (granted to every role that views
  nodes), `disk_encryption:reveal` and `disk_encryption:rotate` (Super
  Admin) and `tang_server:*` (roles with `settings:manage`). New Prometheus
  gauges `bor_luks_volumes_total`, `bor_luks_escrow_operations_total`,
  `bor_luks_recovery_key_reveals_total` and
  `bor_luks_recovery_keys_overdue_total`; the CEF and OCSF exporters map the
  new audit events and `recovery_key` is redacted everywhere.

### Services & Timers Policy Type

- **Services & timers (`Systemd`)** is a new policy type for systemd units
  on nodes. A policy sets, per unit, the enablement (enabled, disabled or
  masked), the activity (running or stopped), overrides for a timer's
  schedule and a service's restart, timeout, environment, resource and
  sandboxing settings through a `90-bor.conf` drop-in, raw directives for
  anything else, and a last-run check for timers and services. Several
  bound policies are merged per unit by binding priority; on equal
  priority the more restrictive value wins. The agent drives systemd over
  D-Bus, records each unit's original state and restores it when the unit
  leaves every policy, re-asserts states on a reconcile pass and within
  seconds of a manual change through systemd's signals, and guards every
  file it writes with the tamper watcher.
- **Scheduled tasks.** A policy can deploy a script or a program as
  `bor-<name>.service` with a timer schedule or a boot trigger, sandboxed
  by default, optionally as an unprivileged user. Failed runs are
  non-compliant with the exit status and the tail of the task's journal.
  The `bor-` prefix is mandatory, so a task can never replace a vendor
  unit.
- **Units of all users.** An entry scoped to *All users* manages the unit
  in every user's `systemd --user` instance: enablement on the file system
  under `/etc/systemd/user` exactly as `systemctl --global` does, drop-ins
  and tasks in the user manager, and the state applied to the sessions that
  are logged in.
- **Preset file.** With the preset switch the agent writes
  `/etc/systemd/system-preset/10-bor.preset`, so the policy's enablement
  decisions also apply to units installed later.
- **Node actions.** The Services & timers section of a node lists the units
  it reported and offers **Start**, **Stop** and **Restart** to holders of
  the new `systemd:operate` permission. The request goes to the agent over
  its policy stream, the row updates with the result, and the server records
  a `systemd.unit_action` audit event. Protected units are refused and risky
  ones ask for a confirmation.
- **Editor.** Unit names come from the inventory agents report; a node
  picker shows what the chosen node does now. Schedule presets, a
  next-runs preview computed by the server's `systemd-analyze`, two
  templates (desktop hardening, maintenance window), a confirmation for
  units whose stop can cut users off (network, SSH, display managers,
  firewall, time sync, audit, cron) and a protected list the server
  refuses (D-Bus, logind, journald, udev, polkit, the boot targets, the
  agent itself).

### SELinux and AppArmor Policy Types

- **SELinux (`Selinux`)** is a new policy type for nodes that run SELinux
  (Fedora, RHEL, SLES 16). A policy sets the enforcement mode (runtime and
  `/etc/selinux/config`), boolean values, per-domain permissive exceptions,
  the enabled state of policy modules, Bor-deployed CIL modules installed
  as `bor-<name>` at semodule priority 450, file contexts with an optional
  relabel, and login mappings to confined SELinux users. Nodes without
  SELinux report the policy inapplicable, or non-compliant when the policy
  requires SELinux; a switch prepares disabled nodes for the next reboot.
  The agent batches every module change of a sync into one `semodule`
  run, records every original value and restores it when the key leaves
  every policy, re-asserts the state on a reconcile pass and within
  seconds of a manual `setenforce`, `setsebool` or `semodule` by following
  the audit records, and guards its files with the tamper watcher.
- **AppArmor (`Apparmor`)** is a new policy type for nodes that run
  AppArmor (Ubuntu, Debian, SLES 15). A policy keeps AppArmor and its
  service on, controls the user namespace restriction of Ubuntu kernels,
  sets profile modes (enforce, complain, disabled) by file name or pattern
  through the parser's `disable/` and `force-complain/` links without
  touching vendor files, deploys custom profiles as `bor-<name>` after a
  parser syntax check, adds site-local rules to vendor profiles inside a
  managed block of their `local/` file, and adds home directory roots.
  Profiles that would share an executable with an existing profile are
  refused, because the kernel would run it unconfined.
- **Editors.** Both editors show, per node or across the fleet, the
  booleans, modules and profiles agents reported, with the server's
  curated list of the switches that matter on desktops and their hardened
  values, one-click templates (process hardening, network homes, kiosk
  accounts, developer workstation; enforce all vendor profiles, user
  namespace stub for an application, confine an application in complain
  mode first, deny network) and confirmations before a permissive mode,
  a disabled profile or a relaxed restriction.
- **Tasks under a profile.** A scheduled task of a Services & timers
  policy can run under an AppArmor profile (`apparmorProfile`, rendered as
  `AppArmorProfile=`) or an SELinux context (`selinuxContext`, rendered as
  `SELinuxContext=`), so a task can use a profile or type that an AppArmor
  or SELinux policy deploys; both editors point at the other.
- **Benchmark controls.** Compliance items that correspond to a CIS
  benchmark control (the SELinux mode and active items, the AppArmor
  enabled and profile items) carry the control's number and title in the
  compliance API and as a label on the Compliance page.
- **Node page.** A new Mandatory access control section shows what a node
  runs (the kernel security module and its mode, the policy or parser
  version, counts per mode), its booleans or profiles, and a summary of
  the recent denials grouped by domain or profile with one redacted
  example. A `userns_create` denial offers the ready stub profile. Holders
  of the new `mac:operate` permission can ask the node for a proposal
  (`audit2allow` output and its CIL translation, or AppArmor rules
  derived from the denials) to review and paste into a policy; nothing is
  applied by a proposal. The nodes list gains a MAC column and filter.

### Software Updates Policy Type

- **Software updates (`Updates`)** is a new policy type that manages the
  distribution's unattended update mechanism and the reboot after
  updates. A policy sets what the node installs on its own (nothing,
  check only, security updates, all updates), the schedule as a drop-in
  of the engine's timer, packages held back, and the reboot rule: never,
  when an update needs it, or after every run, within a daily window,
  only when nobody is logged in unless the reboot has been pending for a
  number of days, with a desktop warning before a reboot that affects
  users. The agent drives `dnf-automatic` (DNF 4 and 5),
  `unattended-upgrades`, `os-update` and rpm-ostree's automatic update
  policy, installs the engine package when it is missing, switches every
  engine's own reboot off and decides reboots itself, records every
  original state and restores it when the node leaves every policy.
- **Node page.** A new Software updates section shows the engine and its
  effective mode, who configured it, the last check and run, the running
  and newest installed kernel, whether a reboot is pending and why, and
  the pending updates with their advisories, severities and CVE ids,
  searchable and filterable to security updates.
- **Compliance.** Items for the engine, the mode, the schedule, the
  reboot rule, each hold and the engine's last run. A policy's **Limits**
  add three age items: a security update pending on the node longer than
  the limit, a reboot pending longer than the limit, and package metadata
  older than the limit (`updates:security-age`, `updates:reboot-age`,
  `updates:check-age`), evaluated after every inventory scan. The mode
  and the age items carry the CIS control *Ensure updates, patches, and
  additional security software are installed* (1.2.2.1 in CIS RHEL 9
  v2.0.0 and CIS Ubuntu 24.04 v1.0.0) on the Compliance page.
- **Node actions.** The Software updates section of a node offers **Check
  for updates** (refresh the metadata and report again), **Install
  updates now** (run the engine once with the policy's mode and show the
  tail of its output) and **Reboot** (at once without sessions; forced,
  with a desktop warning and a one-minute delay, with users logged in).
  They need the new `updates:operate` permission and are audited as
  `updates.action`.
- **Fleet views.** The nodes list has an Updates column and filter
  (security updates pending, reboot pending, no update engine, not
  reported) and the dashboard's fleet overview counts the nodes with
  security updates pending, with a reboot pending and without an engine,
  from a new `GET /api/v1/updates/summary`.
- **Firmware.** Nodes with fwupd list their pending firmware updates in
  the inventory; a policy can enable or disable `fwupd-refresh.timer` and
  report pending firmware as non-compliant (`updates:firmware`). Firmware
  is never installed by policy. Snap packages are out of scope.
- **Offline installs on Fedora.** With **Install offline at the reboot**
  the engine's timer only downloads; the agent stores a dnf5 offline
  transaction and the policy's reboot runs it before the desktop comes
  up. A stored transaction counts as a pending reboot and is removed when
  the policy leaves (`updates:offline` item).
- **Transactional systems.** openSUSE MicroOS, Aeon, Kalpa and SLE Micro
  are driven through `transactional-update` (`/etc/transactional-update.conf`,
  its timer, zypper locks for holds, `/run/reboot-needed` as the reboot
  signal); `updates.engine` in the agent configuration forces an engine.
- **CVE export.** The nodes list and the node section export the pending
  updates as CSV (node, groups, engine, package, version, advisory,
  severity, CVE ids) from `GET /api/v1/updates/export`, and dnf nodes now
  report the CVE ids of their security advisories.
- **Schedule drop-in renamed.** The Software updates type writes its
  timer schedule as `<timer>.d/90-bor-updates.conf` (it was
  `90-bor.conf`, which the Services & timers type removed as one of its
  own stale drop-ins); an agent upgrade replaces the old file.

### KDE Plasma Policy Type Rebuilt

- **Any KDE setting, from a catalogue.** The fixed field list of the KDE
  Plasma (`Kconfig`) type is replaced by generic KConfig entries: any
  configuration file, group path, key and value, with KDE's immutable
  (`[$i]`), shell-expansion (`[$e]`), default (`[$d]`) and locale markers.
  A built-in catalogue of curated settings (session and shell
  restrictions, Plasma desktop, application menu actions, Dolphin, Konsole,
  KRunner, Okular, Ark, KWallet, Kate, Spectacle, KDE PIM, screen lock,
  session, power, appearance, launcher favourites, input and locale,
  privacy, devices, KIO proxy, System Settings and URL rules) documents
  each entry with the file, group and key it writes and the closest Windows
  Group Policy setting. The editor offers a searchable catalogue tree,
  typed value widgets, enforce and expand switches, custom entries, INI
  import, presets (security baseline, shared lab, public kiosk, branding)
  and a rendered-file preview. Policies written by older editors are
  converted when opened and keep working.
- **Settings reported by nodes.** Agents on KDE nodes report the settings
  described by the installed KConfigXT schemas and the System Settings
  modules they have, so a node picker in the editor shows what a given node
  actually offers (`GET /api/v1/kconfig/catalogue`, `/api/v1/kconfig/kcms`).
  With `kconfig.probe_effective` the agent reads the written settings back
  inside a logged-in session and reports user overrides of non-enforced
  defaults as non-compliant.
- **Desktop layout and wallpaper.** A policy can deploy a wallpaper, a
  Plasma panel layout script and an optional base global theme as a
  generated look-and-feel package, applied once to existing users, live to
  logged-in sessions, or enforced as the global theme so that panels and
  wallpaper return to the policy at every login.
- **Application packs.** A Konsole profile (optionally the default and
  locked through Kiosk restrictions), and a list of applications hidden
  from menus and launchers.
- **Scope to Unix groups.** A policy can apply to the members of Unix groups
  only: the agent writes a directory per group, a login hook resolves
  membership by GID and puts the matching directories first in
  `XDG_CONFIG_DIRS`, highest priority first. Group-scoped policies can carry
  their own desktop layout, Konsole profile and hidden applications.
- **Flatpak KDE applications** see the managed configuration through a
  system-wide Flatpak override (`kconfig.flatpak_override`, on by
  default). **Show-only module restrictions** hide every System Settings
  module that is not listed, based on the modules installed on the node.

### Sign-in and MFA

- **The sign-in page asks for the second factor before the password.**
  Enter the user name, then the security key or authenticator code, then
  the password. A security key completes the sign-in on its own. Users
  without a second factor go straight from the user name to the password.
  The API behind it is the multi-step flow `POST /api/v1/auth/begin` and
  `/api/v1/auth/step`; the former `POST /api/v1/auth/login` is still
  served for API clients.
- **MFA enrollment at sign-in.** With **Require MFA for all users** on, a
  user without a second factor can now be guided to set up an authenticator
  app or a security key right after entering the password and only then
  gets a session (**Set up MFA while signing in**, allowed by default; the
  alternative refuses the sign-in).
- **Step-up authentication** re-checks the identity before privileged
  actions, starting with revealing a recovery key: the user gives a reason
  or ticket number (stored in the audit log), the password (checked against
  the directory for LDAP accounts) and an authenticator code, and receives
  a single-use token valid for five minutes and for that one action
  (`/api/v1/auth/step-up`, `/step-up/method`, `/step-up/collect`).
- **Precise session revocation.** Tokens carry their issue time, so
  disabling a user, changing their password or revoking their sessions
  invalidates exactly the tokens issued before that moment.
- **Ready for single sign-on.** User accounts can now be federated to an
  external identity provider: such accounts have no password in Bor, are
  matched by the provider's stable subject and never by email, and their
  groups can be synchronized from the provider. Linking an
  **administrator** account to a single sign-on identity by email needs a
  prior, expiring approval by another administrator (**Allow SSO link** on
  the Users tab, shown once a sign-in connection exists). OIDC and SAML
  sign-in and SCIM provisioning are Bor Enterprise features on top of this
  release.
- **Dedicated user and group audit events.** `user.create`, `user.update`,
  `user.delete`, `user.link_identity`, `user_group.create`,
  `user_group.update`, `user_group.delete`, `user_group.member_add`,
  `user_group.member_remove` and `sso.login_failed` complement the generic
  request log.

### Compliance Reports (Bor Enterprise)

- Compliance reports are implemented by the Bor Enterprise server. The
  community server carries only the web UI pages, which show the Reports
  page on a Bor Enterprise server and a Bor Enterprise notice otherwise;
  it has no report tables, permissions or API. Moving
  from the community server to Bor Enterprise of the same version is an
  installation of the Bor Enterprise server and its license; the report
  tables are created on its first start.
- **Reports** (`Fleet -> Reports`) are point-in-time snapshots of the
  fleet's compliance: the nodes in scope with their posture (disk
  encryption, pending security updates, mandatory access control, agent
  version, connection state), the policies in force with their versions,
  the agent's last result per node and policy with the per-setting items
  and their benchmark control labels, the age of every result, stale and
  unreachable markers, and a compliance score. A report never changes
  after it is generated. Generate one for all nodes or for node groups,
  optionally limited to policy types, with a label and notes.
- **Evidence you can hand over.** Every report is stored as a canonical
  JSON bundle (`bor.report.v1`) whose SHA-256 is recorded with the
  report and in the `report.generate` audit event, so a forwarded audit
  log anchors it outside the database. The hash is re-checked whenever
  the report is opened; a mismatch is shown and audited
  (`report.integrity_failure`). Downloads: the JSON bundle and CSV files
  for results, items, nodes and controls; every download is audited.
- **Permissions** `report:view`, `report:create`, `report:manage` (delete,
  pin, schedules) and `report:attest` (sign-off, waivers), created by the
  Bor Enterprise server. Viewing goes to every built-in role that can view
  compliance; Org Admin and Auditor can generate; Super Admin can delete;
  Super Admin and Auditor can sign off.
- **Retention.** Reports are kept for `reports.retention_days` (1095 by
  default) and purged hourly (`report.purge`); `reports.stale_after`
  (168h) sets the stale and unreachable thresholds; `reports.max_results`
  and `reports.generate_timeout` bound one generation.
- **Frameworks.** Results and settings map to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A,
  NIS2 Art. 21(2) and the CIS RHEL 9 v2.0.0 and Ubuntu 24.04 v1.0.0
  benchmarks; CIS controls apply only on their distribution and only
  where the policy's desired state is evidence for them. A **Controls**
  tab lists them per framework with the results behind each control.
  Every report records the mapping version it was built with.
- **Fresh evidence.** A report can first ask the online agents in scope to
  re-check and wait for them (`reports.refresh_wait`, 60s); the report
  records how many answered.
- **Trend and comparison.** The server stores a daily summary of the fleet
  and of every node group (`reports.daily_summary`); the Reports page and
  the dashboard show the compliance score over 30 days. A **Compare** tab
  lists new failures, fixes and scope changes since an earlier report.
- **Schedules and delivery.** Daily, weekly or monthly reports in a time
  zone, delivered by signed webhook (HMAC-SHA256) or by email with the
  documents attached, through a persistent queue with retries (`reports`
  configuration section or `BOR_REPORT_*` variables; read-only settings
  panel with a test email).
- **Waivers, sign-off and legal hold.** Accepted exceptions with an
  expiry are recorded in the reports they cover; a person other than the
  generator approves or rejects a report with a signed statement over its
  hash (new permission `report:attest`, granted to Super Admin and
  Auditor); pinned reports are kept until unpinned.
- **Documents and SIEM.** A signed PDF/A-2b document (optionally
  time-stamped by an RFC 3161 authority), an OCSF 1.3.0 Compliance Finding
  export, and live forwarding of compliance status changes as OCSF
  findings when the audit log is forwarded in OCSF. `bor-verify` also
  verifies the exported sign-offs.
- **Prometheus metrics.** `bor_compliance_*` metrics for stored reports,
  the newest report per trigger, the fleet score, schedule states and
  overdue schedules, the delivery queue and the signing certificate's
  expiry, with suggested alerts in the monitoring guide.

### Documentation Site

- The user and administrator documentation moved into the repository under
  `doc/` as an MkDocs site, published at [docs.getbor.dev](https://docs.getbor.dev):
  installation, configuration, a page per policy type, operations,
  security and compliance, a permissions reference and developer
  documentation (architecture, building, adding a policy type,
  contributing). The README is slimmed down and points there.

## Security

- **Disk encryption is designed for hostile help desks.** Reveals need a
  dedicated permission, a fresh re-authentication with MFA, and leave an
  audit trail; the reveal endpoint bypasses the generic request log in
  favour of explicit events and sets `Cache-Control: no-store`. Tang
  registry URLs are validated with a strict pattern (http or https, host
  name or IPv4 literal, no credentials, query or fragment) and probes dial
  only approved addresses, refusing loopback, unspecified, link-local,
  multicast and broadcast targets (CodeQL `go/request-forgery`). LUKS2
  header integers are parsed with explicit bit sizes and clamped before
  narrowing.
- **New permissions `mac:author` and `mac:operate`.** Creating, saving,
  importing or releasing an SELinux or AppArmor policy that carries
  administrator-authored policy text (custom modules, file contexts, login
  mappings, permissive domains, custom profiles, local overrides) requires
  `mac:author` on top of the policy permissions; refusals are
  `access_denied` events and every such save and release is audited as
  `policy.mac_custom` with the names and a SHA-256 of each text. Asking a
  node for an SELinux module proposal or an AppArmor rule proposal from
  the node page requires `mac:operate`; every request is audited as
  `mac.action`. Super Admin holds both on upgrade. Nodes can refuse custom
  text with
  `selinux.allow_custom_modules: false` and
  `apparmor.allow_custom_profiles: false`, mode changes with
  `selinux.allow_mode_change: false`, and vendor profile edits stay off
  unless `apparmor.allow_vendor_flag_edits: true`. Denial records are
  aggregated and redacted on the node (no user ids or names, home
  directories collapsed) and only the latest summary per node is kept.
- **Holds are audited.** Creating, saving or releasing a Software updates
  policy that holds packages back from updates is audited as
  `policy.updates_hold` with the patterns, since a hold keeps a vulnerable
  package on every node of a group. Forced reboots and reboots with users
  logged in are off by default, confirmed in the editor, always preceded
  by a warning, and can be refused per node with `updates.allow_reboot:
  false`.
- **New permissions `systemd:exec` and `systemd:operate`.** Creating,
  saving, importing or releasing a Services & timers policy that runs
  commands on nodes (tasks or raw `Exec*` directives) requires
  `systemd:exec` on top of the policy permissions; a draft released by
  someone other than its author is checked too. Every such save and
  release is audited as `policy.systemd_exec` with the task names and a
  SHA-256 of each script; refusals are `access_denied` events. Starting,
  stopping or restarting a unit from the node page requires
  `systemd:operate` and is audited as `systemd.unit_action`. Super Admin
  holds both on upgrade; grant them to other roles explicitly. Nodes can
  refuse tasks altogether with `systemd.allow_tasks: false` and actions
  with `systemd.allow_actions: false`.
- **User-group roles are enforced, and every way of granting them is
  guarded.** Roles assigned to user groups, which the UI has always offered,
  now grant their permissions to the group's members; previously they had no
  effect. **Review your user-group role assignments before upgrading.**
  Assigning a role to a user group and adding a member to a user group are
  privilege-escalation-guarded like direct role assignments: membership
  confers every role of the group, so the caller must already hold all of
  those roles' permissions. A user allowed to manage user groups can no
  longer put themselves, or anyone else, into a group carrying permissions
  they do not have.
- **Old inert scoped role assignments are removed.** Earlier versions
  accepted "organization" and "group" scoped role assignments but never
  enforced them. The upgrade deletes those rows (they granted nothing) so
  they can never turn into live grants; the API now rejects scoped
  assignments with HTTP 400 and the scope selector is gone from the UI.
- **Denied changes are audited.** Refused state-changing requests, including
  privilege-escalation refusals, are recorded as `access_denied` audit
  events with the actor, the permission or guard involved and the reason.
  Removing a user or user-group role assignment writes a `revoke_role` event
  naming the user or group and the role. Both honor the audit
  IP-anonymization setting.
- **TOTP enrollment QR codes** are rendered by the `pquerna/otp` library
  the server already used for the codes themselves; the separate
  `go-qrcode` dependency and its image stack are gone.
- **Services & timers time spans** are parsed with a regular expression
  that cannot backtrack, so a crafted value in a policy cannot stall the
  agent.
- **Dependency advisories** resolved since v0.9.0: `golang.org/x/net`
  (HTML parser advisories, now v0.62.0), `golang.org/x/crypto`,
  `fast-uri` (four host-confusion and scheme advisories, 3.1.9),
  `serialize-javascript` (7.1.4) and the npm advisories of October; Go
  1.26 is now the minimum toolchain. The web bundle's third-party license
  notices are tracked in the repository.

## Reliability

- **Node group changes reach connected agents at once.** Adding a node to
  a group, or removing it, now sends that agent a fresh policy snapshot:
  the group's policies apply (or are withdrawn and their changes undone)
  within seconds instead of at the agent's next reconnect.
- **Restart-safe server state.** Pending enrollment tokens and the policy
  stream revision counter are stored in PostgreSQL, so a restart or upgrade
  no longer invalidates outstanding enrollment tokens, and an agent that
  reconnects after a server restart can no longer be served an incomplete
  policy delta. Only a SHA-256 hash of each enrollment token is stored.
- **Agent packages keep the service across upgrades.** The rpm and deb
  packages stopped and disabled `bor-agent` on every upgrade (the
  preremove script ran unconditionally), so an upgraded node stayed
  without an agent after its next reboot. The scripts now disable the
  unit only on removal and restart an enrolled agent on the new binary
  after an upgrade; upgrading from an earlier package re-enables the unit
  once on nodes that hold an agent certificate.

## Bug Fixes

- **KDE Plasma policies now take effect on real desktops.** The agent
  writes the keys Plasma 5 and 6 actually read (Kiosk action, control
  module and URL restrictions included), merges several bound policies by
  binding priority instead of last-writer-wins, and installs a Plasma
  environment hook (`zz-bor.sh`, ordered after the distribution's own
  scripts so Fedora's defaults survive) that puts the managed directory
  into `XDG_CONFIG_DIRS` of every session. An enforced desktop layout
  sticks at every login, and a wallpaper file that is missing or not
  world-readable on the node is reported instead of silently ignored.
  Catalogue entries that Plasma 6 no longer reads are marked as Plasma 5 or
  KDE 4 only.
- **Firewall policies can start firewalld.** The `ensureEnabled` field of
  a Firewall policy, present since 0.8.0 but inert, now makes the agent
  enable and start `firewalld.service` when it is installed but inactive.
- **PKCS#11 builds.** A server built without `-tags pkcs11` answers a
  PKCS#11 CA configuration with a clear "not compiled in" error instead of
  a generic failure, and the HSM support itself moved to the maintained
  community fork of `crypto11`.
- Deleting a policy binding that does not exist answers 404 instead of 409.
- The web UI no longer ships unreferenced static assets.

## Platform & Dependency Updates

- **Go 1.26** is required to build the server and the agent.
- Server: `google.golang.org/grpc` 1.83.2 -> 1.84.0, `golang.org/x/crypto`
  0.55.0 -> 0.58.0, `golang.org/x/net` 0.58.0 -> 0.62.0, `golang.org/x/sys`
  0.47.0 -> 0.49.0, `golang.org/x/text` 0.41.0 -> 0.43.0,
  `google.golang.org/protobuf` 1.36.11 -> 1.36.12, `go-webauthn/webauthn`
  0.16.3 -> 0.18.2, `go-ldap/ldap` 3.4.14 -> 3.4.15, `lib/pq` 1.11.2 ->
  1.12.3, `prometheus/client_golang` 1.23.2 -> 1.25.0. New:
  `eclipse-keypont/crypto11` (PKCS#11, build tag `pkcs11` only). Removed:
  `yeqown/go-qrcode`, `fogleman/gg`, `golang/freetype`, `golang.org/x/image`.
- Agent: `godbus/dbus` 5.2.2 -> 5.2.4, `google.golang.org/grpc` 1.83.2 ->
  1.84.0 and the shared `golang.org/x/*` modules as above.
- Frontend: PatternFly 6.4 -> 6.7.0, React 19.2.8 -> 19.3.1, `react-router`
  8.3.1 -> 8.5.0, `@simplewebauthn/browser` 13.3 -> 14.0, webpack 5.106 ->
  5.112, `webpack-cli` 7.0.1 -> 7.2.3, `globals` 15 -> 17, plus the
  transitive `fast-uri` and `serialize-javascript` fixes. The KDE catalogue
  is bundled into the UI by a generator (`make kconfig-catalogue`).
- CI: `actions/download-artifact` v8, nfpm installed from its release
  tarball, a GitHub Pages pipeline for the documentation site; Dependabot
  ignores TypeScript major updates.
- Metrics: new `bor_luks_volumes_total`, `bor_luks_escrow_operations_total`,
  `bor_luks_recovery_key_reveals_total` and
  `bor_luks_recovery_keys_overdue_total`; see the monitoring guide.

## Upgrade Notes

- **Agents must be upgraded to v0.10.0** to enforce the Disk encryption,
  Services & timers, SELinux, AppArmor and Software updates policy types
  and the rebuilt KDE Plasma type; older agents ignore policy types they do
  not understand and report no MAC, updates or LUKS inventory. The deploy
  wizard rolls the upgrade out from the server itself.
- Database migrations 000030 to 000046 run automatically on startup:
  000030 the disk encryption tables (`luks_volumes`,
  `node_disk_encryption`, `luks_recovery_keys`, `tang_servers`) and the
  `disk_encryption:*` and `tang_server:*` permissions; 000031 the
  persisted enrollment tokens and policy hub revision; 000032 removes the
  inert scoped role bindings and forbids new ones; 000033 the policy owner
  column (existing policies get their creator recorded where the account
  still exists); 000034 federated identities; 000035 externally managed
  user groups; 000036 SSO link approvals; 000037 and 000038 the KDE catalogue, node-reported
  settings and look-and-feel inventory; 000039 the systemd unit inventory;
  000040 and 000041 the `systemd:exec` and `systemd:operate` permissions;
  000042 the mandatory access control inventory (`node_mac_status`,
  `node_mac_items`, `lsm` columns on nodes); 000043 and 000044 the
  `mac:operate` and `mac:author` permissions; 000045 the Software updates
  inventory (`node_updates_status`, `node_updates_pending`); 000046 the
  `updates:operate` permission. The compliance report tables and
  permissions belong to the Bor Enterprise server and are created by it.
- New server settings: `BOR_ESCROW_KEK_FILE`, `BOR_ESCROW_KEK_ID`,
  `BOR_ESCROW_KEK_PREVIOUS_FILES`, `BOR_ESCROW_REQUIRE_MFA`,
  `BOR_ESCROW_RETIRED_RETENTION_DAYS` and
  `BOR_ESCROW_ORPHAN_RETENTION_DAYS`. Disk encryption escrow stays off
  until a KEK file is configured. See `.env.example` and the server
  configuration reference.
- Agent configuration gains the `disk_encryption` section (`state_file`,
  `bootstrap_dir`, `run_dir`, tool paths), new `kconfig` keys
  (`data_path`, `probe_effective`, `flatpak_override`, `write_kde5rc`),
  the `systemd` section (`system_dir`, `preset_dir`, `scripts_dir`,
  `state_path`, `job_timeout`, `reconcile_interval`, `watch_signals`,
  `allow_tasks`, `analyze_binary`, `user_dir`, `user_preset_dir`,
  `allow_actions`), the `selinux` section (`config_path`, `modules_dir`,
  `module_priority`, `state_path`, `reconcile_interval`,
  `allow_mode_change`, `allow_custom_modules`, `follow_audit`,
  `tool_timeout`), the `apparmor` section (`profiles_dir`,
  `parser_binary`, `sysctl_path`, `state_path`, `backup_dir`,
  `reconcile_interval`, `allow_custom_profiles`,
  `allow_vendor_flag_edits`, `follow_audit`, `tool_timeout`), the shared
  `mac` section (`inventory_interval`, `denial_window`, `collect_denials`,
  `allow_actions`) and the `updates` section (`engine`, `state_path`,
  `backup_dir`, `reconcile_interval`, `inventory_interval`,
  `reboot_check_interval`, `tool_timeout`, `allow_install`,
  `allow_reboot`); every key has a working default.
- Agents report the node's kernel security module (`lsm`, `lsm_mode`) in
  the heartbeat; nodes running an older agent show no MAC value until
  they are upgraded.
- Packaging: the agent's deb package now depends on `needrestart`, the rpm
  package recommends `dnf5-plugins` and `python3-dnf-plugins-core`, so a
  node can always tell whether an update needs a reboot; both recommend
  `cryptsetup` and suggest `clevis-luks`, `clevis-dracut` and `tpm2-tools`
  for disk encryption.
- The protobuf policy schema gained `disk_encryption.proto`,
  `systemd.proto`, `selinux.proto`, `mac.proto` and `updates.proto` (policy
  fields 22 to 26), new stream event types for disk encryption tasks,
  systemd, MAC and updates actions, the `lsm` heartbeat fields and a much
  larger `kconfig.proto`; regenerate any external tooling built against
  `proto/`.
- Packagers: the build command is unchanged (`go build ./cmd/server`, with
  `-X main.Version=...`), but needs Go 1.26. `make server-pkcs11` builds
  the HSM variant with cgo.
- API clients: the web UI signs in through `POST /api/v1/auth/begin` and
  `/api/v1/auth/step`; `POST /api/v1/auth/login` keeps working. Role-binding
  requests without `scope_type` (or with `"global"`) behave as before; any
  other scope type is rejected with 400. Adding a role or a
  member to a user group answers 403 when it would grant permissions the
  caller does not hold. Deleting a policy binding that does not exist now
  answers 404 instead of 409.

name: Release v0.9.0
body:
## New Features

### Session Access Policy Type

A new `SessionAccess` policy type controls **when** selected users or groups
may use a desktop session — for example a school computer lab usable only
during school hours, or a kiosk restricted to business hours.

- **Weekly schedules** per user or group: allowed time windows by day, with
  node-local times and midnight-crossing windows (e.g. `22:00`–`02:00`).
- **Two enforcement layers:**
  - *Layer 1 (logind, always on)* — as an allowed window ends the agent warns
    the user (default 30/15/5 minutes, the final warning bypassing
    do-not-disturb) and then **locks** the screen (apps keep running) or
    **logs off** the session, per rule. A re-lock watchdog keeps a session
    locked outside its allowed hours.
  - *Layer 2 (`pam_time`, optional)* — blocks fresh logins outside the allowed
    hours by managing a marked block in `/etc/security/time.conf` and enabling
    `pam_time` in the account stack. Optionally extends to SSH. The block
    encodes the full weekly schedule, so it keeps enforcing even while the
    agent is not running.
- **Distro-aware PAM:** on Debian/Ubuntu the agent enables `pam_time`
  automatically via `pam-auth-update`; on authselect-managed Fedora/RHEL it
  reports a degraded compliance state with a documented one-time admin step
  while Layer 1 still enforces.
- **Lockout guard rails:** `root` is never restricted, the `time.conf` block is
  written atomically with a self-check and is tamper-protected, and unbinding
  the policy removes all PAM artifacts fail-open.
- **Web UI:** a dedicated editor with per-rule user/group lists, a day-and-time
  window builder, lock/log-off selection, warning thresholds, the PAM and SSH
  switches, and a node-requirements info box.

Known limitation, by design: on GNOME and KDE the **screen unlock** is enforced
by the Layer-1 watchdog, not PAM — the desktop lockers do not honour the PAM
account phase on unlock. Use the **Log off** end action with PAM for the
strictest restriction. See `docs/session-access.md` for full behaviour, the
node requirements, and break-glass recovery.

### Flatpak Policy Type and Application Catalog

A new `Flatpak` policy type manages Flatpak remotes and applications on
managed desktops, with a server-side application catalog.

- **Remotes:** configure any number of Flatpak remotes per policy (URL, GPG
  key, subset such as Flathub's `verified`, allow-/deny-list filters,
  priority, enabled state). Definitions are written to `/etc/bor/flatpak/`
  and tamper-protected; existing remotes such as a distribution-provided
  `flathub` are adopted rather than duplicated and restored on unbind.
- **Applications:** desired state *Present*, *Latest* or *Absent* per app,
  with remote, branch, *optional* and *delete data* flags. The agent drives
  the `flatpak` CLI idempotently, off the policy stream, with per-operation
  timeouts (default 30 minutes), and reports one compliance item per remote
  and per application.
- **Updates:** optional periodic `flatpak update` and unused-runtime cleanup.
- **Not applicable when Flatpak is absent:** nodes without `flatpak` report
  the policy as Inapplicable, like other unsupported subsystems.
- **Catalog (Settings → Flatpak repositories):** Flathub is indexed out of
  the box from its AppStream feed; additional repositories can be added from
  a `.flatpakrepo` URL or manually, refreshed on a schedule or by uploading
  an `appstream.xml.gz` for air-gapped servers. The policy editor searches
  the catalog and copies remote definitions into the policy, so policies stay
  self-contained. New permissions `flatpak_repo:*` (backfilled onto every
  role that holds `settings:manage`); new server settings
  `BOR_FLATPAK_CATALOG_REFRESH`, `BOR_FLATPAK_CATALOG_MAX_DOWNLOAD_MB` and
  `BOR_FLATPAK_CATALOG_ALLOW_PRIVATE_NETWORKS`.
- **Agent config:** optional `flatpak:` section (`binary`, `state_dir`,
  `state_file`, `proxy_url`).

See [`docs/flatpak.md`](docs/flatpak.md).

### Instance-Hosted Agent Packages and Deploy Wizard

Every Bor server now ships and serves the agent packages itself, so managed
nodes never need internet access to install or upgrade the agent.

- The `bor-server` packages and the container image embed the `bor-agent`
  packages for all formats (deb, rpm, apk, Arch) and architectures (amd64,
  arm64, ppc64le) under `/usr/share/bor/agent-repo`, assembled and
  GPG-signed at release build time.
- The server serves them at `/agent/*`: a signed flat apt repository
  (`/agent/deb`), a signed dnf/zypper repository (`/agent/rpm`), direct
  downloads for Alpine and Arch, the repository signing key
  (`/agent/repo-key.asc`), the internal CA certificate (`/agent/ca.crt`) and a
  static install page at `/agent/`. Download endpoints are public by design
  (package managers cannot authenticate); files are served through a rooted
  filesystem with no directory listings.
- **Deploy agent wizard** (download icon in the masthead, or the button on the
  Nodes page): pick the platform (Debian/Ubuntu, RHEL/Fedora, SUSE, Alpine,
  Arch) and architecture and get a single copy-paste script that trusts the
  server CA, sets up the signed repository or downloads the package, and
  optionally generates a one-time enrollment token inline so the same script
  enrolls and starts the agent. A *Direct downloads* tab lists every package.
- New setting `BOR_AGENT_REPO_DIR` (`agent_repo.dir`); when the directory
  holds no manifest the feature is off and `/agent/*` returns 404. The server
  logs a warning at startup when the packaged agent version differs from its
  own.
- New Prometheus counter `bor_agent_package_downloads_total{format,arch}`
  (aggregate labels only, no client identifiers).

### Policy Export and Import

Policies can be exported and imported as `bor.dev/v1` YAML bundles
(schema in `proto/export/export.proto`), for backups, migration between
servers and keeping policies in version control.

- **Format:** Kubernetes-style envelope — one `Policy` or `PolicyBinding`
  document per YAML document, with `metadata.name` / `displayName` /
  `description` and a `spec` holding the policy type and its canonical
  content. Bindings reference policies by slug or display name and node
  groups by name, never by UUID, so bundles are portable across servers.
- **Export** from the Policies list: a single policy from its kebab menu, or
  select several and export them as one bundle with their bindings. The API
  (`GET /api/v1/policies/export`) also supports `format=json`.
- **Import** (`POST /api/v1/policies/import`): uploading a bundle first runs a
  **dry run** and shows a preview table of what would be created, updated,
  skipped or rejected; nothing is written until confirmed. Conflict modes
  for an existing policy name: fail the import (default), skip that policy,
  or update the existing draft (released policies are never overwritten).
  A bundle with any invalid document is rejected as a whole, and bindings
  to node groups that do not exist on the server are reported as errors.
- Export requires `policy:view`, import requires `policy:create`; both are
  audited (`policy.export`, `policy.import`).

### Policy Creation Wizard

- `/policies/new` is now a four-step wizard: **Type** (tiles grouped into
  Browsers / Desktop / System, each with a tagline and a description panel),
  **Details** (name, description), **Configuration** (the same editor used on
  the edit page) and **Review**. A contextual help drawer is available on
  every step after the first.
- The success screen offers the two things people do next — **Release now**
  (with confirmation) and **Assign to a node group**, which opens the binding
  form with the new policy pre-selected — plus open the editor, create another
  or back to the list. Changing the type after configuring or leaving with
  unsaved work asks for confirmation.
- Policy types now have a single registry (labels, taglines, descriptions,
  icons) used by the wizard, the Policies list, the dashboard and the
  bindings page; Firefox, Chrome, Thunderbird, KDE and Flatpak show their
  brand marks (CC0-licensed) next to the type name.
- Internally the monolithic policy editor was split into shared per-type
  editors (tree editors for the browser catalogues, KConfig, JSON-backed
  types), so the wizard and the edit page cannot drift apart.

### Readable Sidebar and Masthead in Every Theme

- The sidebar and masthead are now styled through per-theme semantic
  properties, so navigation group titles, the current item, the footer and
  links stay readable in the light, dark and high-contrast themes (group
  titles 7.9:1, links 9.4:1, footer 6.6:1 in the light theme; previously as
  low as 1.65:1). Fixes #138.
- De-emphasized text (policy descriptions, meta rows) is standardized at
  14 px with a theme-aware subtle token instead of hand-rolled small gray
  text.

## Security

- **Flatpak catalog SSRF hardening** (CodeQL `go/request-forgery`): admin-
  supplied repository URLs are validated with a strict https-only pattern
  (host name or IPv4 literal, no credentials); loopback, unspecified,
  link-local, multicast and broadcast addresses are always refused and
  private/CGNAT ranges are refused unless
  `BOR_FLATPAK_CATALOG_ALLOW_PRIVATE_NETWORKS=true`; the transport resolves
  names itself and dials only approved addresses (DNS pinning), TLS 1.2
  minimum.
- **Agent package downloads** are served through an `os.Root`-scoped
  filesystem (path traversal and symlink escapes are structurally
  impossible), never list directories, set `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`
  and cap manifest reads. Only public material (CA certificate, signing
  public key) is exposed.
- **Release signing:** the agent repository signing key may now be
  passphrase-protected; the passphrase is consumed from the environment
  only and never passed on a command line.
- **Dependabot:** all open alerts resolved — gRPC-Go HTTP/2 DATA-frame
  memory exhaustion (GHSA-vp52-pcj8-j9qc), five `fast-uri` host-confusion /
  SSRF advisories, two `browserslist` advisories, `brace-expansion`,
  `js-yaml`, `nanoid` and `postcss-selector-parser`.

## Bug Fixes

- Dashboard: nodes without a group and the per-group online/offline tiles
  are computed from the many-to-many `node_group_ids` array; previously every
  node was reported as unassigned and the group tiles stayed empty. A node in
  several groups is now counted in each.
- Policies: the Polkit editor no longer crashes on rules created through the
  API, where protojson omits empty `action_ids` / `action_prefixes` /
  `action_conditions` arrays; sparse rules are normalized on load.
- Agent: the systemd unit sets `TimeoutStopSec=120` so long-running
  enforcement steps (Flatpak installs, package transactions) can wind down
  cleanly on stop instead of being killed.
- Compose: `BOR_VERSION` build argument sets the version shown in the sidebar
  and `/api/v1/version`.

## Platform & Dependency Updates

- Server + agent: `google.golang.org/grpc` 1.82.1 → 1.83.2,
  `golang.org/x/crypto` 0.52.0 → 0.55.0, `golang.org/x/net` 0.55.0 → 0.58.0,
  `golang.org/x/text` 0.39.0 → 0.41.0, `golang.org/x/sys` 0.45.0 → 0.47.0.
  Server: `github.com/go-ldap/ldap/v3` 3.4.12 → 3.4.14. Agent:
  `google.golang.org/protobuf` 1.36.11 → 1.36.12.
- Frontend: `react-router` 8.3.0 → 8.3.1 plus the transitive `fast-uri`,
  `browserslist`, `postcss-selector-parser`, `js-yaml`, `brace-expansion`
  and `nanoid` bumps.
- CI: `actions/checkout` v7; the pipeline gained an *Assemble Agent Repo*
  stage between the agent and server package builds, and the container image
  embeds the assembled repository. Dependabot ignores ESLint major updates
  until `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` supports ESLint 10.
- Metrics: new `bor_flatpak_catalog_apps_total`,
  `bor_flatpak_catalog_last_success_timestamp`,
  `bor_flatpak_catalog_refresh_total` and
  `bor_agent_package_downloads_total`; see `docs/metrics.md`.

## Notes

- Agents must be upgraded to v0.9.0 to enforce the new SessionAccess and
  Flatpak policy types; older agents ignore policy types they do not
  understand. The new deploy wizard is the easiest way to roll the upgrade
  out from the server itself.
- Database migration `000029_flatpak_catalog` runs automatically at server
  start: it adds the `flatpak_repositories`, `flatpak_catalog_apps` and
  `flatpak_catalog_icons` tables, the `flatpak_repo:*` permissions and the
  seeded Flathub repository.
- The protobuf policy schema gained `session_access.proto` and
  `flatpak.proto` (policy fields 20 and 21) and a new
  `proto/export/export.proto`; regenerate any external tooling built against
  `proto/`.
- New server settings: `BOR_AGENT_REPO_DIR`, `BOR_FLATPAK_CATALOG_REFRESH`
  (set to `false` on air-gapped servers; catalog uploads still work),
  `BOR_FLATPAK_CATALOG_MAX_DOWNLOAD_MB` and
  `BOR_FLATPAK_CATALOG_ALLOW_PRIVATE_NETWORKS`. See `.env.example` and
  `server/server.yaml.example`.
- Servers built from source or from a container build that did not run the
  release pipeline contain no agent repository; the deploy wizard and
  `/agent/*` stay off until a packaged build is installed.
- SessionAccess Layer 2 (`pam_time`) requires `systemd-logind` and PAM on the
  node; on authselect-managed Fedora/RHEL a one-time admin step is needed and
  the agent reports the policy as degraded until it is done.

name: Release v0.8.0
body:
# Release v0.8.0

## New Features

### Thunderbird Policy Type

Manage Mozilla Thunderbird on enrolled desktops with the same mechanism used for Firefox ESR.

- Agent writes the managed `policies.json` that Thunderbird expects, merged from all bound policies; removing the last policy restores the original file.
- Flatpak installations are detected and enforced alongside RPM/DEB installations.
- Managed files carry a "managed by Bor" marker and are protected by the tamper watcher — external edits are detected and immediately restored.
- Web UI: full policy editor with the complete Thunderbird policy catalogue.

### Microsoft Edge for Business Policy Type

- Agent writes `bor_managed.json` into each Edge managed-policy directory; removing the last bound policy cleans the file up from every directory.
- Web UI: tree-based editor with the Edge policy catalogue, JSON validation, and setting preview before enabling.

### Firewalld Zone Policy Type

- New `Firewalld` policy type manages firewalld zones on enrolled nodes: services, ports, forward ports, rich rules, masquerade, interfaces, sources, and zone target.
- Agent writes zone XML to `/etc/firewalld/zones/`, validates with `firewall-cmd --check-config`, and reloads firewalld; files are tamper-protected like all other managed files.
- Web UI: dedicated firewalld zone editor.

### Polkit: Variable Conditions

- Polkit rules now support variable conditions via `action.lookup()` for matching on action variables.
- Fix: multiple action IDs in one rule are now correctly joined with `||`.

### Per-Action RBAC for Users and Roles

- User and role administration is now guarded by per-action permissions instead of a single blanket permission, allowing finer-grained delegation of admin duties.

### Web UI Overhaul (UX Sprints 0–4)

A full modernization pass over the PatternFly 6 web interface:

- **URL routing** — every page now has a real URL with working browser back/forward and deep links; expired sessions are detected and redirected to login; a global error boundary prevents white-screen crashes.
- **Full-page policy editor** — the policy editor is now a routed page (`/policies/:id/edit`) instead of nested modals; the Package editor's nested tabs were flattened into disclosures.
- **Policy safety rails** — unsaved-changes guard, confirmation for destructive type changes, JSON validation for Chrome/Edge values, read-only Configuration view for released policies, and setting preview in the tree editors.
- **Policy lifecycle from the list** — release/unrelease policies directly from the Policies list view.
- **Scalable lists** — server-side pagination, filtering, and sorting for Nodes and Compliance; search, sorting, and empty states across all list pages; dashboard stat tiles link to pre-filtered lists and keep last-good data on transient refresh errors.
- **Destructive-action protection** — type-to-confirm dialogs for all resource deletes, plus server-side guards that prevent deleting, disabling, or demoting the last Super Admin.
- **MFA usability** — backup codes can be copied/downloaded and must be acknowledged before finishing enrollment; the MFA settings tabs were disambiguated.
- **Login** — password reveal toggle and Caps Lock hint.
- **Navigation** — sidebar grouped into Fleet / Policy / System; single left-aligned page title with subtitle.
- **Quality-of-life** — searchable dropdowns, editable node notes, kebab menu on policy bindings, theme-aware audit-log status badges.
- **Accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA)** — accessible tree roles in the policy editors, `aria-live` status messages, focus-ring and dark-mode/high-contrast correctness via PatternFly 6 design tokens, and an `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` lint gate in CI. See `docs/ACCESSIBILITY.md` for the compliance record.

### Proto-Driven Policy Catalogues

- The Firefox, Thunderbird, Chrome, and Edge policy catalogues shown in the web UI are now generated from protobuf annotations — one source of truth shared by server, agent, and frontend.

## Security

This release includes a dedicated hardening pass:

- Agent identity is now strictly bound to the mTLS client certificate, and MFA/RBAC enforcement paths were hardened on the server.
- Legacy SHA-256-encrypted TOTP secrets are transparently migrated to HKDF-derived encryption on first read.
- The Ubuntu PPA and Fedora COPR repository import helpers now block redirect-based SSRF; only allowlisted redirect targets are followed.
- Audit log CSV export is guarded against spreadsheet formula injection.
- The auto-generated initial admin password is no longer printed to the server log (where it would land in journald/centralized logging); it is written to a root-only file (mode 0600) instead.
- PKI: the server TLS certificate is automatically regenerated when its SANs no longer match the configured hostnames.
- All open Dependabot alerts were resolved, including the react-router RSC CSRF advisory (GHSA-qwww-vcr4-c8h2) fixed by the react-router 8 upgrade.

## Bug Fixes

- Dashboard keeps showing the last good data during transient refresh errors instead of flashing empty.
- Audit log default action badge uses a fixed gray with sufficient dark-mode contrast.
- CI: nfpm pinned to v2.46.3 to stay compatible with the Go 1.25 toolchain.

## Platform & Dependency Updates

- Frontend: React 18.3 → 19.2, `react-router-dom` replaced by `react-router` 8.3, PatternFly 6.6 prop migration, TypeScript typecheck now enforced in CI.
- Server + agent: `google.golang.org/grpc` → 1.82.1, `golang.org/x/crypto` → 0.52.0, `golang.org/x/net` → 0.55.0, `golang.org/x/text` → 0.39.0.
- CI: frontend design-token guardrail (bans legacy `--pf-v5-*` variables, ratchets raw hex literals), accessibility lint gate.

## Notes

- Agents must be upgraded to v0.8.0 to enforce the new Thunderbird, Edge, and Firewalld policy types; older agents ignore policy types they do not understand.
- The protobuf policy schema gained `thunderbird.proto` and `firewalld.proto` and extends the polkit and edge messages; regenerate any external tooling built against `proto/policy/`.
- Frontend development now requires Node.js 22.22+ (react-router 8 engines requirement).

name: Release v0.7.0
body:
## New Features

###   Package Management Policy
  
  This release introduces a new `Package` policy type, enabling administrators to manage software repositories and packages on enrolled Linux desktops.

  ---
  Features
  
  Agent: Package enforcement via PackageKit

  - Package installation, removal, and "keep at latest" enforcement via the PackageKit (https://www.freedesktop.org/software/PackageKit/) D-Bus API — abstracts APT, DNF, and Zypper uniformly across distributions.
  - Auto-detects the node's package manager (APT / DNF / Zypper) to write the correct repository file format.
  - Writes APT deb822 .sources files to /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ and GPG keys to /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/.
  - Writes DNF/YUM .repo INI files to /etc/yum.repos.d/ and RPM GPG keys to /etc/pki/rpm-gpg/.
  - Writes Zypper .repo INI files to /etc/zypp/repos.d/.
  - Repository and package state is merged from multiple bound policies by priority (higher-priority bindings win conflicts).
  - Desktop notifications inform the user when package policy changes are applied.

  Web UI: Package Policy Editor

  - Repositories tab — add, edit, and remove repositories per type (APT deb822, DNF, Zypper). Fields adapt to the selected type. GPG key upload supported for all types.
  - Packages tab — manage packages with desired state (present / absent / latest), optional version pinning, and an "optional" flag.
  - Options tab — control cache refresh after repo writes and allow-downgrade behaviour.

  Web UI: Repository import helpers

  Three one-click import flows are available in the Repositories tab:

  - Add Ubuntu PPA… — enter a ppa:owner/name address and select an Ubuntu codename; the server fetches the repository URI and signing key from Launchpad and the Ubuntu keyserver automatically.
  - Add openSUSE 1-Click .ymp… — upload a .ymp file; the server parses the XML and populates repositories and packages. When the file contains multiple distversion groups, a selection modal lets you choose which to import.
  - Add Fedora COPR… — enter a owner/project or @group/project address and select a chroot; the server resolves the DNF repo URL and signing key from the COPR API.

  ---
  Notes
  
  - GPG verification is enabled automatically when a signing key is fetched successfully; it is disabled (with a warning) when no key is available, so the repository is still added and usable.
  - The .ymp importer skips type="pattern" items (not installable via PackageKit) and reports them as warnings.
  - Signed-off builds require godbus/dbus/v5 as a new agent dependency.

name: Release v0.6.0
body:
## New Features
  
  - ACME / Let's Encrypt support — the server can now automatically provision and renew TLS certificates from Let's Encrypt or any RFC 8555-compatible CA. Enabled with BOR_ACME_ENABLED=true + BOR_ACME_DOMAINS + BOR_ACME_EMAIL. Mutually exclusive with manually supplied cert/key files.
  - Self-service password management — users can now change their own password from the Account Security settings in the UI without administrator involvement. Admins can also reset other users' passwords from the Users tab.

## Bug Fixes

  - WebAuthn origin fallback — WebAuthn no longer silently fails to initialize when BOR_WEBAUTHN_ORIGINS is not set. The server now derives a default origin of https://<RPID>, so standard deployments on port 443 only need BOR_WEBAUTHN_RPID.
  - Agent module consistency — agent/go.mod indirect dependencies (x/net, x/sys, x/text) are now in sync with the golang.org/x/crypto bump applied by Dependabot, resolving go mod tidy build failures.

## Dependency Updates

  - golang.org/x/crypto → 0.51.0 (server + agent)
  - google.golang.org/grpc → 1.81.0 (agent)
  - github.com/Azure/go-ntlmssp → 0.1.1 (server)
  - github.com/fsnotify/fsnotify → 1.10.1 (agent)
  - golang.org/x/image → 0.38.0 (server)
  - Frontend: ts-proto, webpack, babel-loader, postcss, fast-uri
  - CI: actions/upload-artifact v7, docker/login-action v4, softprops/action-gh-release v3
